nameStory: The 'marsh' part of this plant's name tells you exactly where to find it - in wet, soggy places where many plants can't survive. 'Hedge nettle' comes from its traditional use growing along hedgerows, though unlike true stinging nettles, this mint family member won't burn your skin when you touch it.
description: Marsh hedge nettle is a sturdy perennial wildflower that thrives in New England's wettest spots. Growing 2-3 feet tall, it sends up square stems topped with spikes of purple and white flowers in summer. Despite its intimidating name, this plant is actually quite gentle to touch and belongs to the same family as your kitchen herbs like basil and oregano.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Purple and white flowers cluster in dense spikes at the top of stems in mid-summer, with the classic two-lipped shape of mint family flowers

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Fuzzy, soft-feeling leaves grow opposite each other on the stem and feel noticeably hairy or 'pubescent' when you rub them between your fingers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Stems are distinctly square when you roll them between your fingers - a telltale sign of the mint family - and usually grow straight up without branching

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: The entire plant has a distinctly fuzzy, almost woolly feel due to fine hairs covering stems, leaves, and even the flower parts

habitat: Look for marsh hedge nettle in New England's consistently moist areas like stream banks, wet meadows, and the edges of marshes and swamps. It thrives in rich, muddy soils that stay damp through the growing season, often growing alongside other water-loving plants like cattails and sedges.

seasonality.spring: New fuzzy shoots emerge from the wet soil as temperatures warm, with the distinctive square stems becoming apparent early on.
seasonality.summer: Mid-summer brings the showy purple and white flower spikes that make identification easiest, blooming from July into August.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and small nutlets develop while leaves may yellow and begin to die back as wetland areas fluctuate with seasonal rains.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back completely to underground roots, leaving no above-ground trace until spring returns.

funFact: Despite being called a 'nettle,' this plant is actually more closely related to the mint in your tea than to stinging nettle - and botanists have discovered four brand new species in this confusing genus just in the southeastern US during the 2010s alone!
confusionNotes: Marsh hedge nettle is easily confused with its close relative marsh woundwort, but feel the leaves - marsh hedge nettle has much fuzzier, more pubescent foliage that's noticeably soft to the touch, while marsh woundwort feels smoother.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - 'hedge nettles' won't sting you like true nettles do. The taxonomy of eastern hedge nettles is still being sorted out by botanists, so you might find conflicting information in different field guides as scientists work to understand these closely related species.
compareHints: Among New England's hedge nettles, marsh hedge nettle stands out for its exceptionally fuzzy, soft-textured leaves and stems compared to its smoother relatives. It was historically considered just a variety of another species until botanists recognized its consistently more pubescent nature and unbranched growth habit as distinctive enough to warrant its own species status.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its hedge-nettle relatives, this species stands out for its narrow, hyssop-like leaves and preference for wetter habitats.
Marsh woundwort differs from its hedge-nettle cousins by its preference for consistently wet habitats rather than just moist woodland edges.
Unlike other hedgenettles in New England, woolly hedgenettle is the only one with thick, densely woolly leaves that feel soft to touch.
Prairie woundwort differs from marsh woundwort by preferring dry rather than wet habitats and having broader, more heart-shaped leaves.
